summary: This program defines a function that takes two pieces of information — a list of food items and a table number — and prints out a delivery report for Beepo the robot waiter. The function is then called twice with different orders, showing how one definition can be reused for many situations.

lines.text: Defines the function with two parameters separated by a comma, so each call must supply both a food list and a table number.

lines.code: """Helps Beepo the robot waiter deliver food to a table."""
lines.text: A docstring: a short sentence in triple quotes that records what the function is for, so anyone reading the code later knows its purpose.
An f-string drops the value of table_number straight into the message, giving each call its own heading.
Loops over the items in the list that was passed in, so the function works whether the order has two dishes or ten.
The two leading spaces and dash indent each dish underneath the heading, making the output read like a printed order slip.
The \n adds a blank line after the confirmation so consecutive deliveries do not run together on screen.
Calls the function with the list as the first argument and the table number as the second; order matters, because Python matches arguments to parameters by position.
A second call with completely different data proves the point of writing a function: the logic is written once and reused.
